analysis.title: The great AI unwind: capitulation or the next buying opportunity
key_insights: NDX has been stuck in a range since May. 29k in futures is the make-or-break level, with the 200-day moving average just below at about 28,500.
GS reports roughly $20bn of TMT selling over two weeks. Global tech selling hit a -3.3 sigma extreme. Fundamental net exposure is at YTD lows, while gross exposure is at the 63rd percentile.
The GS Risk Appetite Indicator had one of its largest drops on record, to its lowest level since April 2025. Net exposure is depressed, but gross exposure is the real source of pain.

GS sees similarities between last week's tech unwind and July's selloff. About $20bn of TMT was sold over two weeks versus $23bn in July. SPX fell 2.4% versus 3.4% in July. AI stocks are moving together more, but index volatility is contained.

The NDX/SPX volatility spread rose to the 98th percentile of its five-year range. Thursday's widening was the second largest in five years. Tech-specific fear is expensive relative to broad market volatility, which GS frames as a potential relative-value opportunity.

AI demand remains robust but financing is more expensive. More than $500bn of AI infrastructure debt was absorbed this year, and hyperscaler funding costs rose about 120bps per JPM. Google, Microsoft and Amazon results are key this week, mainly for how backlog converts to revenue and how the next leg of investment is financed.

JPM argues the widening in AI-related CDS spreads mostly reflects banks buying protection against growing data center exposure, not deteriorating fundamentals. The gap between CDS and cash bonds is creating potential relative-value opportunities.

JPM highlights Nvidia's financing relationships with GPU customers such as CoreWeave as a possible transmission channel for credit stress. A financing squeeze among GPU operators could feed back into their suppliers.

TS Lombard says tech exports are about 40% of GDP in Taiwan and nearly 20% in Korea. An AI capex slowdown could hit Asian export economies harder, and the stimulus to the US economy may be smaller than headline spending suggests.

TS Lombard's Dario Perkins argues an AI bust could benefit the broader economy. The AI boom adds to inflation and keeps rates higher, squeezing housing and other rate-sensitive sectors. If AI capex collapses, the Fed could cut aggressively and help non-tech demand.

JPM remains constructive on tech fundamentals but flags unsustainable semiconductor pricing and neocloud financing stress. Software looks relatively resilient. JPM sees early November as a potential buying window, conditional on positioning capitulating, hyperscalers confirming capex, semiconductor earnings holding up and credit spreads tightening. SOX is testing its 200-day moving average.

tension_points.bull_case: Positioning has washed out, with $20bn of TMT sold and fundamental net exposure at YTD lows. JPM remains constructive on tech fundamentals and sees early November as a buying window.
tension_points.bear_case: Gross exposure is still at the 63rd percentile, AI financing costs are up about 120bps, and credit stress could pass through Nvidia's customer financing. SOX is testing its 200-day moving average.
tension_points.what_invalidates: JPM's buying window requires positioning to capitulate, hyperscalers to confirm capex, semiconductor earnings to hold up and credit spreads to tighten. Failure on these conditions invalidates it.

tension_points.bull_case: TS Lombard argues an AI capex collapse would let the Fed cut aggressively, reviving rate-sensitive sectors that missed out on the boom.
tension_points.bear_case: The US stimulus from AI spending may be smaller than headline figures suggest, and Asian export economies would be hit disproportionately.
